A proud son of Ngāti Manawa, war veteran Richard Dargaville, once a soldier for the New Zealand Army, he remains forever a soldier for te ao Māori. His service reflects not just commitment to a nation, but a deep dedication to whakapapa, identity, and the ongoing struggles and strengths of his whānau and wider Māori communities. (R)

Through the act of karanga, we traverse both the physical and spiritual realms, guided by ancestral voices that echo through time. This sacred practice is far more than a ritual—it is a powerful form of cultural expression that binds the living with those who have passed on. Within the context of Whiria te hono, a distinguished collective of kaikaranga from Ngāti Whātua Ōrākei, the spiritual and practical responsibilities of this tradition are deeply honoured and carefully upheld. These wāhine carry the weight of generations with each call, embodying the values, stories, and mana of their iwi. (R)

Charlie Rahiri describes himself as a reluctant iwi leader. But he was destined by his kaumātua to lead his iwi, Ngati Ranginui. He’s a direct descendant of Iwi chief Paraone Koikoi who surrendered his guns and pouches to the colonial office in 1864, only to be back in his kainga in Taumata three years later fighting for his land by pulling up survey pegs. We look at the changing role of a Māori Leader in Modern society through the eyes of Charlie Rahiri. (R)
